title: Valorant Star Banned After Former PC Owner’s Cheating Scandal Uncovered – Kotaku Report
body:
A German Valorant competitor has been banned after Riot Games’ Vanguard anti‑cheat system flagged his computer as compromised—not because of anything he did, but due to remnants left by the previous owner of his Ryzen 7 processor. The case, which quickly went viral on gaming forums, highlights the growing complexity of hardware‑based detection methods and raises fresh questions about consumer responsibility, privacy and the limits of anti‑cheat technology.

The player, who goes by the in‑game name “Eclipse”, purchased a second‑hand desktop that included a high‑end AMD Ryzen 7 CPU. Within weeks of joining the competitive scene, Vanguard flagged his system for “unauthorized software” and issued a permanent ban. When Eclipse appealed, Riot’s investigation revealed that hidden files and modified firmware—traces of a cheat program used by the PC’s former owner—remained embedded in the processor’s microcode. According to Riot’s technical team, the anti‑cheat software scans for signatures at the hardware level, and the lingering code was enough to trigger a violation. The only remedy offered was a complete hardware replacement, effectively forcing the player to discard the entire machine.

Riot’s stance is rooted in the evolution of anti‑cheat strategies that have moved beyond simple software scans. Vanguard, introduced in 2020, operates with kernel‑level access and can query low‑level system components, including CPU microcode, BIOS, and driver signatures. This depth allows it to detect sophisticated cheats that hide in firmware or modify hardware behavior. However, the approach also creates a gray area: legitimate users may become collateral damage if a previous owner’s modifications are not fully removed. The company’s policy, outlined in its public anti‑cheat guidelines, states that any detection of prohibited code—regardless of who installed it—constitutes a breach of the Terms of Service.

The incident has sparked a broader debate within the gaming community about the responsibilities of second‑hand hardware buyers. While many gamers assume that a fresh installation of the operating system and a clean drive are sufficient, the reality may be more complex. “People often think they can wipe a hard drive and be safe,” said Dr. Lena Hoffmann, a cybersecurity researcher at the Technical University of Munich. “Modern cheats can embed themselves in firmware, which isn’t overwritten by a simple OS reinstall. Without specialized tools, those remnants can persist indefinitely.”

Consumer‑rights advocates argue that penalizing players for hardware they did not tamper with could be unfair and potentially illegal under certain jurisdictions. In Germany, where data protection and consumer protection laws are stringent, the case may set a precedent. Legal experts suggest that Riot could face challenges if it cannot demonstrate that the detection was accurate and that the player had a reasonable opportunity to remediate the issue without a full hardware swap. Some have called for a more nuanced ban system that distinguishes between active cheating and inherited contamination.

For developers, the episode serves as a cautionary tale about the balance between aggressive anti‑cheat enforcement and user goodwill. While protecting the integrity of competitive play is essential, overly punitive measures risk alienating a portion of the player base, especially those who purchase budget or refurbished equipment. Riot has indicated that it is reviewing its policies to provide clearer guidance on how to cleanse hardware of hidden cheat signatures, potentially offering a verification service or a whitelist process for affected users.

Looking ahead, the gaming industry is likely to see increased collaboration between hardware manufacturers and anti‑cheat providers to create tamper‑proof environments that can be reliably audited. As cheat developers continue to innovate, anti‑cheat solutions will need to evolve, but they must also incorporate safeguards that protect innocent users from unintended consequences. For now, Eclipse’s experience serves as a stark reminder that in the era of firmware‑level cheating, the phrase “clean slate” may require more than just a fresh install—it may demand a brand‑new machine.
